sectionTitle: How bonding and structure are related to the properties of substances
topic: How bonding and structure are related to the properties of substances

specStatements.text: The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. Melting and freezing take place at the melting point, boiling and condensing take place at the boiling point.

The three states of matter can be represented by a simple model. In this model, particles are represented by small solid spheres. Particle theory can help to explain melting, boiling, freezing and condensing.

The amount of energy needed to change state from solid to liquid and from liquid to gas depends on the strength of the forces between the particles of the substance. The nature of the particles involved depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance. The stronger the forces between the particles the higher the melting point and boiling point of the substance.
(HT only) Limitations of the simple model above include that in the model there are no forces, that all particles are represented as spheres and that the spheres are solid.
Students should be able to:
predict the states of substances at different temperatures given appropriate data
explain the different temperatures at which changes of state occur in terms of energy transfers and types of bonding
recognise that atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of materials
(HT only) explain the limitations of the particle theory in relation to changes of state when particles are represented by solid inelastic spheres which have no forces between them.
In chemical equations, the three states of matter are shown as (s), (l) and (g), with (aq) for aqueous solutions.
Students should be able to include appropriate state symbols in chemical equations for the reactions in this specification.
Ionic compounds have regular structures (giant ionic lattices) in which there are strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions between oppositely charged ions.
These compounds have high melting points and high boiling points because of the large amounts of energy needed to break the many strong bonds.
When melted or dissolved in water, ionic compounds conduct electricity because the ions are free to move and so charge can flow.
Knowledge of the structures of specific ionic compounds other than sodium chloride is not required.
Substances that consist of small molecules are usually gases or liquids that have relatively low melting points and boiling points.
These substances have only weak forces between the molecules (intermolecular forces). It is these intermolecular forces that are overcome, not the covalent bonds, when the substance melts or boils.
The intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.
These substances do not conduct electricity because the molecules do not have an overall electric charge.
Students should be able to use the idea that intermolecular forces are weak compared with covalent bonds to explain the bulk properties of molecular substances.

Polymers have very large molecules. The atoms in the polymer molecules are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds. The intermolecular forces between polymer molecules are relatively strong and so these substances are solids at room temperature.
Students should be able to recognise polymers from diagrams showing their bonding and structure.

Substances that consist of giant covalent structures are solids with very high melting points. All of the atoms in these structures are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds. These bonds must be overcome to melt or boil these substances. Diamond and graphite (forms of carbon) and silicon dioxide (silica) are examples of giant covalent structures.
Students should be able to recognise giant covalent structures from diagrams showing their bonding and structure.
Metals have giant structures of atoms with strong metallic bonding. This means that most metals have high melting and boiling points.
In pure metals, atoms are arranged in layers, which allows metals to be bent and shaped. Pure metals are too soft for many uses and so are mixed with other metals to make alloys which are harder.

Metals are good conductors of electricity because the delocalised electrons in the metal carry electrical charge through the metal. Metals are good conductors of thermal energy because energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of the structures of specific ionic compounds other than sodium chloride is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Sodium chloride is the only ionic compound whose structure is described or pictured anywhere in this topic. Other ionic compounds are named only where the property being tested follows from the general statements of 4.2.2.3 - that ionic compounds form giant lattices with strong electrostatic attraction in all directions, have high melting and boiling points, and conduct when molten or dissolved in water. No question asks for the arrangement, coordination number, unit cell or lattice type of magnesium oxide, calcium fluoride or any other named ionic compound, and no such structure is taught in the concepts.

concepts.definition: The state in which particles are packed closely in a fixed arrangement, so a solid keeps its own shape and volume.
The state in which particles are still close together but can move past one another, so a liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.
The state in which particles are far apart and move randomly, so a gas fills whatever container it is put in.
The one temperature at which a substance melts and at which it also freezes. Solid to liquid and liquid to solid both happen at this temperature.
The one temperature at which a substance boils and at which it also condenses. Liquid to gas and gas to liquid both happen at this temperature.

concepts.term: Simple model of the three states
concepts.definition: A model in which the particles of a substance are represented by small solid spheres, arranged closely and regularly in a solid, closely but randomly in a liquid, and far apart in a gas.
The attractions holding the particles of a substance to one another. Their strength depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance.
The energy that must be supplied to separate particles from one another. The stronger the forces between the particles, the more energy is needed and the higher the melting point and boiling point.
(HT only) In the simple model there are no forces between the particles, all particles are shown as spheres, and the spheres are shown as solid.
A property such as melting point, colour, hardness or electrical conductivity that belongs to a large collection of particles arranged in a structure, not to a single atom.
The letter or letters written in brackets after a formula in a chemical equation to show the state of that substance: (s) for solid, (l) for liquid and (g) for gas.
A solution made by dissolving a substance in water. It is shown in an equation by the state symbol (aq).
The regular structure formed by an ionic compound, in which very many oppositely charged ions are held in a repeating three-dimensional arrangement.
The attraction between oppositely charged ions. In a giant ionic lattice these forces are strong and act in all directions.

concepts.term: High melting and boiling points of ionic compounds
concepts.definition: Ionic compounds melt and boil at high temperatures because large amounts of energy are needed to break the many strong bonds in the lattice.
When an ionic compound is melted or dissolved in water the ions become free to move, so charge can flow and the substance conducts electricity.
A substance whose particles are small groups of atoms joined by covalent bonds. Such substances are usually gases or liquids with relatively low melting and boiling points.
The weak force of attraction between one molecule and another. It is these forces, not the covalent bonds, that are overcome when a molecular substance melts or boils.
A strong bond formed by a shared pair of electrons between two atoms inside a molecule.
Molecules are neutral, so a molecular substance has no charged particles that are free to move and it does not conduct electricity.
Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.
A substance whose molecules are very large. The atoms in a polymer molecule are joined to other atoms by strong covalent bonds, usually forming a long chain.

concepts.term: Why polymers are solids at room temperature
concepts.definition: Because polymer molecules are very large, the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong, so polymers are solids at room temperature.
A structure in which all of the atoms are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds throughout the whole structure. These bonds must be overcome to melt or boil the substance.
Diamond and graphite, which are forms of carbon, and silicon dioxide, also called silica.
The strong bonding in the giant structure of atoms that makes up a metal. It means that most metals have high melting and boiling points.

concepts.term: Layers of atoms in a pure metal
concepts.definition: In a pure metal the atoms are arranged in layers. The layers can slide over one another, which allows metals to be bent and shaped.
A mixture of a metal with other metals. Pure metals are too soft for many uses, so they are mixed to make alloys, which are harder.
Electrons in a metal that are free to move through the whole structure. They carry electrical charge through the metal, so metals conduct electricity well.
Metals are good conductors of thermal energy because energy is transferred through the metal by the delocalised electrons.
A substance is solid below its melting point, liquid between its melting point and its boiling point, and gas above its boiling point.

misconceptions.question: Does a substance have a freezing point that is a different temperature from its melting point?
misconceptions.correct: No. Melting and freezing both take place at the melting point.
misconceptions.misconception: Each named change of state has its own temperature, so a substance has four different values: a melting point, a freezing point, a boiling point and a condensing point.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language gives every change its own name, so students assume every name must come with its own number. Data books quote only two values and students do not notice that the other two are not missing.
misconceptions.correction: There are only two temperatures. At the melting point the change can go either way, and at the boiling point the change can go either way. Ice melts at 0 degrees C and water freezes at 0 degrees C.

misconceptions.question: A gas is cooled until it becomes a liquid. Is this freezing?
misconceptions.correct: No, it is condensing, and it happens at the boiling point.
misconceptions.misconception: Freezing and condensing are the same cooling change, so a liquid turns into a solid at the boiling point rather than at the melting point.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link cooling with freezing because that is what a freezer does, so both cooling changes get the same name and the same temperature.
misconceptions.correction: Cooling a gas to a liquid is condensing and takes place at the boiling point. Cooling a liquid to a solid is freezing and takes place at the melting point.

misconceptions.question: In the simple model, do the spheres show what particles really look like?
misconceptions.correct: No. The spheres are only a representation of the particles.
misconceptions.misconception: The drawn spheres show the real shape, real size and real appearance of the particles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams are drawn confidently and to a neat scale, so students read them as pictures rather than as models.
misconceptions.correction: In the model particles are represented by small solid spheres. Real atoms are not solid spheres and are far too small to be drawn to scale.

misconceptions.question: When a solid melts, do the particles themselves change?
misconceptions.correct: No. The particles stay the same; their arrangement and movement change.
misconceptions.misconception: The particles soften, swell or melt as the substance melts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer what they can see happening to the whole lump onto the single particle, so the particle is imagined melting too.
misconceptions.correction: Melting changes only the arrangement and the movement of the particles. Each particle is unchanged before and after the change of state.

misconceptions.question: Does melting or boiling break the particles into smaller pieces?
misconceptions.correct: No. A change of state separates particles from each other; it does not break them up.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating a substance until it melts or boils splits its particles into smaller particles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both processes are described as things being 'broken', so breaking forces and breaking particles are treated as the same event.
misconceptions.correction: A change of state overcomes the forces holding particles together. The particles themselves survive unchanged, which is why the change can be reversed by cooling.

misconceptions.question: Does a substance melt at a high temperature because its particles are heavy?
misconceptions.correct: No. It melts at a high temperature because the forces between its particles are strong.
misconceptions.misconception: Heavier particles always mean a higher melting point.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass is easier to picture than force, and heavier objects are harder to lift, so students transfer that feeling to particles.
misconceptions.correction: The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles, which depends on the type of bonding and the structure, not on particle mass.

misconceptions.question: When a molecular substance boils, are covalent bonds broken?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the weak intermolecular forces between the molecules are overcome.
misconceptions.misconception: Boiling or melting a molecular substance breaks the covalent bonds inside its molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know covalent bonds are the bonds in a molecular substance, so when energy is supplied they assume those are what the energy breaks.
misconceptions.correction: The molecules stay intact. Steam is still made of H2O molecules. It is the intermolecular forces between molecules that are overcome when the substance melts or boils.

misconceptions.question: Does a substance boil at a higher temperature simply because it was heated for longer?
misconceptions.correct: No. The boiling point depends on the strength of the forces between the particles.
misconceptions.misconception: The longer a substance is heated, the higher the temperature at which it boils.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students confuse the time taken to reach the boiling point with the value of the boiling point itself.
misconceptions.correction: The boiling point is a fixed property of the substance. Heating for longer supplies more energy but does not change the temperature at which the substance boils.

misconceptions.question: (HT) Is the main limitation of the simple model that it draws too few particles?
misconceptions.correct: No. The listed limitations are that there are no forces, all particles are spheres, and the spheres are solid.
misconceptions.misconception: The model fails mainly because a diagram shows only a handful of particles instead of billions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students notice the obvious visual shortcut first, because the number of circles on the page is easy to count.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists three limitations: the model has no forces, all particles are represented as spheres, and the spheres are solid. The number drawn is only a convenience of the diagram.

misconceptions.question: (HT) Can the simple model explain changes of state at all?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, in part; it explains arrangement and movement but not the energy needed.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the model has limitations it is useless, and it cannot explain melting or boiling at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Once students learn a model is limited they treat it as wrong, rather than as useful within a boundary.
misconceptions.correction: The model explains the arrangement and movement of particles in each state well. What it cannot explain is why energy is needed to change state, because it includes no forces.

misconceptions.question: (HT) Why does a model with no forces struggle to explain boiling?
misconceptions.correct: Because boiling means overcoming forces, and the model contains none.
misconceptions.misconception: The problem is that the spheres are drawn too large compared with real atoms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Scale errors are visible on the page, while the absence of forces is invisible, so the visible fault is picked.
misconceptions.correction: If there were genuinely no forces between the particles, no energy would be needed to separate them and a substance would have no fixed boiling point at all.

misconceptions.question: A substance is above its melting point. Must it be a gas?
misconceptions.correct: No. Above the melting point but below the boiling point it is a liquid.
misconceptions.misconception: When deciding the state from melting- and boiling-point data, students compare the temperature against only one of the two values instead of both, then read that single comparison off wrongly (e.g. above the melting point means gas, below the boiling point means solid), so they misclassify the state.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students use one value instead of two, checking only whether the temperature is above the number they looked at first.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the temperature with both values: below the melting point it is solid, between the two it is liquid, and above the boiling point it is a gas.

misconceptions.question: A substance has a melting point of -219 degrees C and a boiling point of -183 degrees C. Is it solid at 20 degrees C?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a gas, because 20 degrees C is above -183 degrees C.
misconceptions.misconception: Negative melting and boiling values mean the substance is a cold solid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The minus sign is read as 'cold', and cold is associated with solids such as ice, so the negative numbers are taken as evidence of a solid.
misconceptions.correction: A negative boiling point means the substance boils far below room temperature, so at 20 degrees C it is already a gas.

misconceptions.question: Should you assume a substance is a liquid at room temperature unless told otherwise?
misconceptions.correct: No. The state must be worked out from the melting point and boiling point data.
misconceptions.misconception: Substances are liquids at room temperature unless there is a reason to think otherwise.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most laboratory chemicals students meet are in bottles of solution, so liquid feels like the default state.
misconceptions.correction: Always compare room temperature with both quoted values. Room temperature is just another temperature to place on the scale.

misconceptions.question: Is the difference between the melting points of sodium chloride and chlorine caused by the number of bonds alone?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is caused by the type of bonding and the strength of the forces to be overcome.
misconceptions.misconception: All bonds are about equally strong, so a substance with fewer bonds simply melts sooner.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bonds are usually drawn as identical lines, so students count them rather than compare their strengths.
misconceptions.correction: Different types of bonding give forces of very different strengths. Strong electrostatic attraction in an ionic lattice needs far more energy to overcome than weak intermolecular forces.

misconceptions.question: Is one copper atom shiny, bendable and a good conductor?
misconceptions.correct: No. These are bulk properties of the metal structure, not of a single atom.
misconceptions.misconception: A single atom has the same properties as the material it comes from.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that a material is made only of its atoms, so each atom must contain the material's properties in miniature.
misconceptions.correction: Properties such as shine, malleability and conductivity arise from how very many atoms are arranged and bonded together. A lone atom has no layers to slide and no delocalised electrons to move through.

misconceptions.question: Does (aq) mean that a substance is a liquid?
misconceptions.correct: No. It means the substance is dissolved in water.
misconceptions.misconception: The symbol (aq) is used for any liquid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Solutions are poured like liquids, so students treat (aq) and (l) as interchangeable ways of saying the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: (l) means the pure substance itself is liquid, such as water at room temperature. (aq) means the substance is dissolved in water to form an aqueous solution.

misconceptions.question: Does (aq) mean pure water?
misconceptions.correct: No. It labels the dissolved substance, not the water.
misconceptions.misconception: The symbol (aq) is a way of writing water into an equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word aqueous is heard as a synonym for water, so the symbol is attached to the solvent rather than to the solute.
misconceptions.correction: (aq) is written after the formula of the substance that is dissolved. Water itself, when it is a product or reactant in its own right, is written H2O(l).

misconceptions.question: How should a piece of magnesium ribbon be labelled in an equation?
misconceptions.correct: As Mg(s), because it is a solid.
misconceptions.misconception: A metal that is about to react in a solution should be written as (aq).
misconceptions.whyItArises: The metal is dropped into a solution, so students label it with the state of the mixture rather than the state of the metal itself.
misconceptions.correction: The state symbol describes the substance as it is at the start of the reaction. Magnesium ribbon is a solid, so it is Mg(s), even though it is added to a solution.

misconceptions.question: How is the water made in a neutralisation reaction labelled?
misconceptions.correct: As H2O(l).
misconceptions.misconception: Water in an equation is written as H2O(aq).
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate water with the symbol (aq) because (aq) means dissolved in water, so the two are merged.
misconceptions.correction: Water produced in a reaction is a pure liquid, so it takes (l). The symbol (aq) is reserved for a substance dissolved in water.

misconceptions.question: How is dilute hydrochloric acid labelled in an equation?
misconceptions.correct: As HCl(aq), because it is dissolved in water.
misconceptions.misconception: Dilute acid is written HCl(l) because it can be poured.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students choose the state symbol by looking at the bottle rather than by asking what is dissolved in what.
misconceptions.correction: Dilute acids are solutions of the acid in water, so they always take (aq). Only a pure liquid substance takes (l).

misconceptions.question: Does solid sodium chloride contain NaCl molecules?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a giant ionic lattice of sodium ions and chloride ions.
misconceptions.misconception: An ionic solid is made of separate molecules of the compound stuck together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The formula NaCl looks like the formula of a molecule, and molecules are the first particles students meet.
misconceptions.correction: In the lattice every sodium ion is surrounded by chloride ions and every chloride ion by sodium ions. NaCl gives the ratio of ions, not a molecule.

misconceptions.question: Is each sodium ion attracted to just one chloride ion?
misconceptions.correct: No. Each ion is attracted to all the oppositely charged ions around it.
misconceptions.misconception: Ions pair up, one positive with one negative, and the pairs then stack together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bonding diagrams show a single electron transfer between one atom and one other, so students keep those two particles paired for good.
misconceptions.correction: In a giant ionic lattice the electrostatic forces of attraction act in all directions between oppositely charged ions, which is what makes the structure so strong.

misconceptions.question: Do the electrostatic forces in an ionic lattice act in only some directions?
misconceptions.correct: No. They act in all directions between oppositely charged ions.
misconceptions.misconception: The forces act only along the rows of the lattice, like bonds drawn between neighbours.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Lattice diagrams are drawn with straight lines between nearest neighbours, which look like directional bonds.
misconceptions.correction: Electrostatic attraction acts in all directions around every ion. The lines in a diagram show the arrangement, not a limited set of bonds.

misconceptions.question: Do ionic compounds melt at high temperatures because their ions are heavy and tightly packed?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is because large amounts of energy are needed to break the many strong bonds.
misconceptions.misconception: The lattice is hard to melt because the ions are heavy and squashed together with no room to move.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Close packing is visible in a diagram, whereas the strength of an electrostatic force is not, so packing is used as the explanation.
misconceptions.correction: The high melting point comes from the many strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions. Breaking them needs a large amount of energy.

misconceptions.question: What carries the charge when molten sodium chloride conducts?
misconceptions.correct: The ions, which are free to move.
misconceptions.misconception: Electrons are released when the compound melts, and those electrons carry the charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conduction is first taught for metals, where electrons are the charge carriers, so the same explanation is reused for every conductor.
misconceptions.correction: Ionic compounds contain ions, not free electrons. When melted or dissolved the ions become free to move and so charge can flow.

misconceptions.question: Are ions made when an ionic compound melts or dissolves?
misconceptions.correct: No. The ions are already present in the solid; melting or dissolving only frees them to move.
misconceptions.misconception: Melting or dissolving splits neutral atoms or molecules up into ions for the first time.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students connect conduction with ions and know the solid does not conduct, so they conclude the ions cannot have been there before.
misconceptions.correction: The solid is already a lattice of ions, but they are held in fixed positions. Melting or dissolving allows them to move, so charge can flow.

misconceptions.question: Does a solution conduct because water is a good conductor?
misconceptions.correct: No. It conducts because the dissolved ions are free to move.
misconceptions.misconception: Water conducts electricity, so any solution will conduct.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Safety warnings about water and electricity teach students that water conducts, and the warning is remembered as chemistry.
misconceptions.correction: Pure water is a very poor conductor. A salt solution conducts because dissolving separates the ions and lets them move and carry charge.

misconceptions.question: Are substances made of small molecules gases because their molecules are light?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is because the forces between the molecules are weak.
misconceptions.misconception: Light molecules float away as a gas; heavy ones sink together as a solid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience of balloons and smoke links lightness with rising, and rising with being a gas.
misconceptions.correction: The state depends on whether the intermolecular forces are strong enough to hold the molecules together at that temperature, not on how heavy each molecule is.

misconceptions.question: Are there any forces between the molecules of a molecular substance?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, weak intermolecular forces act between them.
misconceptions.misconception: Molecular substances have covalent bonds inside the molecules and nothing at all between them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Intermolecular forces are not drawn on dot and cross diagrams, so students conclude there is nothing there.
misconceptions.correction: Weak intermolecular forces do act between molecules. If there were none, every molecular substance would be a gas at every temperature.

misconceptions.question: When water boils, are both the covalent bonds and the intermolecular forces overcome?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the intermolecular forces are overcome.
misconceptions.misconception: Boiling overcomes the forces between molecules and also breaks some of the bonds inside them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students who have been told covalent bonds are strong still expect a share of the energy to go into breaking them.
misconceptions.correction: Boiling water gives steam, which is still made of H2O molecules. The covalent bonds inside each molecule are untouched.

misconceptions.question: Does boiling water produce hydrogen and oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: No. It produces steam, which is still water.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating water enough splits the molecules into hydrogen and oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both processes involve heating and both are described as things coming apart, so a change of state is confused with a chemical change.
misconceptions.correction: Boiling is a physical change that separates whole molecules from one another. Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen needs electrolysis, not boiling.

misconceptions.question: Where do intermolecular forces act?
misconceptions.correct: Between one molecule and another.
misconceptions.misconception: Intermolecular forces are the forces holding the atoms together inside a molecule.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The prefix inter- is confused with intra-, and both words describe attraction, so the two are swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Intermolecular means between molecules. The forces inside a molecule are the covalent bonds, which are much stronger.

misconceptions.question: Why does a larger molecule usually have a higher boiling point?
misconceptions.correct: Because the intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: Because a larger molecule has more covalent bonds inside it that must be broken.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly notice that a larger molecule has more bonds, then apply that count to the wrong forces.
misconceptions.correction: The covalent bonds are not broken on boiling. Larger molecules simply attract one another more strongly, so more energy is needed to separate them.

misconceptions.question: Why does liquid octane not conduct electricity?
misconceptions.correct: Because its molecules have no overall electric charge.
misconceptions.misconception: Because it contains no metal atoms, or because liquids cannot conduct at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conduction is first met in metals and in solids, so students rule out anything that is neither.
misconceptions.correction: Conduction needs charged particles that are free to move. Molecules are neutral overall, so a molecular substance has no charge to carry, whatever its state.

misconceptions.question: Are polymer molecules joined to each other by covalent bonds?
misconceptions.correct: No. Covalent bonds join atoms within a molecule; the molecules attract one another by intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.misconception: One polymer chain is bonded covalently to the next chain, which is why polymers are solid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know polymers are strong and that covalent bonds are strong, so the strength is credited to covalent bonds everywhere.
misconceptions.correction: Within a polymer molecule the atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds. Between molecules the intermolecular forces are relatively strong because the molecules are very large.

misconceptions.question: Is a polymer a giant covalent structure like diamond?
misconceptions.correct: No. A polymer is made of separate very large molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: Polymers and giant covalent structures are the same thing because both contain many covalent bonds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are drawn as large networks of atoms, and both are solids, so the two categories are merged.
misconceptions.correction: In diamond every atom is linked to other atoms throughout the whole structure. A polymer consists of separate long molecules held to each other by intermolecular forces.

misconceptions.question: A diagram shows a long chain of atoms joined by covalent bonds, continuing at both ends. What is it?
misconceptions.correct: A polymer molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: A chain of atoms in a diagram must be a metal or a single small molecule.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students match diagrams to the picture they saw most recently rather than reading the bonding and the continuation marks.
misconceptions.correction: Continuation marks at both ends show a very large molecule made of a repeating unit joined by covalent bonds, which is a polymer.

misconceptions.question: Why does silicon dioxide have a very high melting point?
misconceptions.correct: Because strong covalent bonds throughout the structure must be overcome.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the intermolecular forces between its molecules are unusually strong.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that covalent substances melt at low temperatures because of weak intermolecular forces, then apply that rule to every covalent substance.
misconceptions.correction: Silicon dioxide has no separate molecules. All of its atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds, and those bonds must be overcome to melt it.

misconceptions.question: Is diamond held together by attraction between charged particles?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is held together by strong covalent bonds between neutral carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Giant structures with high melting points must be ionic lattices.
misconceptions.whyItArises: High melting point and the word giant are first met with ionic compounds, so the pairing is remembered as a rule.
misconceptions.correction: Diamond, graphite and silicon dioxide are giant covalent structures. Their high melting points come from covalent bonds, not from charges.

misconceptions.question: Do metals melt at high temperatures because they are hard?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is because the metallic bonding in the giant structure is strong.
misconceptions.misconception: Hard materials melt at high temperatures and soft materials melt at low ones.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hardness and melting point are both loosely described as strength, so the two properties are treated as one.
misconceptions.correction: Sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife yet still a metal with metallic bonding. Melting point depends on the strength of the bonding, not on hardness.

misconceptions.question: Is an alloy a compound?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a metal mixed with other metals.
misconceptions.misconception: The metals in an alloy react together to make a new compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect two substances put together and heated to react, and the alloy has properties neither metal had.
misconceptions.correction: An alloy is a mixture. Its atoms are of different sizes, which distorts the layers and stops them sliding, so the alloy is harder than the pure metal.

misconceptions.question: Why is an alloy harder than the pure metal?
misconceptions.correct: Because atoms of different sizes disrupt the layers, so they cannot slide over one another.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the alloy contains more delocalised electrons, which make the bonding stronger.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Delocalised electrons are the explanation students remember for metals, so they are used for every metallic property.
misconceptions.correction: Hardness here is about the layers. Different sized atoms distort the regular layers of a pure metal and stop them sliding.

misconceptions.question: What carries the electric charge through a metal?
misconceptions.correct: The delocalised electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: The metal ions move through the structure and carry the charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conduction in molten ionic compounds is explained by moving ions, so the same explanation is reused for metals.
misconceptions.correction: In a solid metal the positive ions stay in place in the giant structure. It is the delocalised electrons that move and carry charge through the metal.

misconceptions.question: Do protons carry the charge in a metal wire?
misconceptions.correct: No. The delocalised electrons do.
misconceptions.misconception: Because protons are positive, they must be what flows in a wire.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate current with positive charge from circuit diagrams and conclude that the positive particles must be moving.
misconceptions.correction: Protons are held in the nuclei of the metal ions and cannot move. Only the delocalised electrons are free to move through the metal.

misconceptions.question: Why do metals conduct thermal energy well?
misconceptions.correct: Because energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Because the atoms are packed so tightly that energy is passed straight along.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Close packing is easy to picture, and it does play a part in non-metals, so it is offered as the whole explanation.
misconceptions.correction: In a metal the delocalised electrons move quickly through the structure and transfer energy, which is why metals conduct thermal energy far better than non-metals.

misconceptions.question: Do a material's properties appear only once its atoms have joined into a compound?
misconceptions.correct: No. They arise from how very many atoms are arranged and bonded in a structure.
misconceptions.misconception: A lone atom has no properties, but as soon as atoms combine chemically the properties appear.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that compounds have different properties from their elements, and generalise this into a rule that properties come from combining rather than from structure.
misconceptions.correction: Copper is an element, not a compound, yet a piece of copper is shiny, malleable and conducting. The properties come from the giant structure of many atoms, whether the substance is an element or a compound.

mcqs.stem: At which temperature does a liquid change into a solid?

options.text: At its melting point, the same value as for melting
options.rationale: Melting and freezing both take place at the melting point.

options.text: At its freezing point, a lower value than melting
options.rationale: Students who expect every named change to have its own temperature invent a freezing point below the melting point.

options.text: At its boiling point, where condensing happens
options.rationale: Freezing and condensing are both cooling changes, so the boiling point is offered for both.

options.text: At any temperature far below room warmth
options.rationale: Freezing is judged by how cold the surroundings feel rather than against the substance's own melting point.

mcqs.stem: Bromine vapour is cooled until it becomes a liquid. Which change of state is this, and at which temperature does it happen?

options.text: Condensing, at the condensing point of bromine
options.rationale: A separate temperature is invented for each named change of state.

options.text: Condensing, at the boiling point of bromine
options.rationale: Boiling and condensing both take place at the boiling point.

options.text: Freezing, at the melting point of bromine
options.rationale: Every cooling change is labelled freezing, so the melting point is chosen.

options.text: Condensing, at bromine's melting point
options.rationale: The change is named correctly but paired with the wrong one of the two quoted temperatures.

mcqs.stem: In the simple model of the three states of matter, how are the particles represented?

options.text: As spheres drawn to the true size of an atom
options.rationale: The diagram is read as a picture of reality rather than as a model.

options.text: As spheres that swell when the solid melts
options.rationale: What happens to the whole sample is transferred onto the individual particle.

options.text: As small solid spheres of the same kind
options.rationale: The specification states that in this model particles are represented by small solid spheres.

options.text: As tiny cubes stacked in a neat grid
options.rationale: The regular arrangement of a solid is confused with the shape used for the particles.

mcqs.stem: A solid is heated until it melts. Using the simple particle model, what happens to the particles?

options.text: They soften and change into smaller spheres
options.rationale: The melting of the lump is imagined happening to each particle as well.

options.text: They break up into several smaller particles
options.rationale: Breaking forces between particles is confused with breaking the particles apart.

options.text: They lose their shape and flow into each other
options.rationale: The bulk behaviour of a liquid is attributed to the individual particles.

options.text: They stay the same but move further apart
options.rationale: A change of state alters the arrangement and movement of the particles, not the particles themselves.

mcqs.stem: Substance X melts at 801 degrees C and substance Y melts at -7 degrees C. What does this tell you about the two substances?

options.text: The particles in X must be much heavier than in Y
options.rationale: Mass is used in place of force as the reason for a high melting point.

options.text: The forces between the particles in X are much stronger
options.rationale: The stronger the forces between the particles, the higher the melting point.

options.text: Substance Y has no forces between its particles
options.rationale: A low melting point is read as meaning there is nothing holding the particles together.

options.text: Y has stronger forces, so it melts much sooner
options.rationale: The relationship is inverted: an easier melt is taken to mean stronger attraction.

mcqs.stem: Why do some substances need much more energy to boil than others?

options.text: Because the particles they contain are larger and heavier
options.rationale: Particle mass is treated as the property that sets the boiling point.

options.text: Because they have to be heated for a much longer time
options.rationale: Time taken to reach the boiling point is confused with the value of the boiling point.

options.text: Because the forces between their particles are stronger
options.rationale: The energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles.

options.text: Because a greater mass of substance is being used
options.rationale: The amount of substance is confused with a property of the substance.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) Which of these is a limitation of the simple model of the three states of matter?

options.text: The model draws far too few particles to be realistic
options.rationale: The most visible shortcut in the diagram is picked instead of the listed limitations.

options.text: The model cannot explain any melting or boiling at all
options.rationale: A limited model is treated as useless rather than useful within a boundary.

options.text: The model shows solid, liquid and gas apart
options.rationale: A feature that is simply how the diagram is laid out is offered as a flaw.

options.text: The model shows no forces between the particles
options.rationale: The specification lists the absence of forces as one of the limitations of the simple model.

mcqs.stem: (HT only) In the simple model the particles are solid inelastic spheres with no forces between them. Why does this make boiling hard to explain?

options.text: Boiling overcomes forces the model leaves out
options.rationale: Energy is needed at the boiling point to overcome forces between particles, and the model contains no forces.

options.text: The spheres are drawn much larger than real atoms
options.rationale: A visible scale fault is chosen instead of the missing forces.

options.text: The model uses far fewer particles than a real sample
options.rationale: The number of particles drawn is offered as the reason the model fails.

options.text: The particles in the model move much too slowly
options.rationale: The speed of the particles is invented as a fault of the model.

mcqs.stem: Ethanol melts at -114 degrees C and boils at 78 degrees C. What is the state of ethanol at 25 degrees C?

options.text: Gas, because 25 degrees C is above the melting point
options.rationale: Only one of the two values is used, so anything above the melting point is called a gas.

options.text: Solid, because 25 degrees C is far below 78 degrees
options.rationale: The boiling point alone is used, and below it is read as solid.

options.text: Liquid, because 25 degrees C lies between the two values
options.rationale: A substance is a liquid between its melting point and its boiling point.

options.text: Liquid and gas together in about equal amounts
options.rationale: A single temperature is imagined giving a mixture of two states.

mcqs.stem: Substance P has a melting point of -219 degrees C and a boiling point of -183 degrees C. What is the state of P at 20 degrees C?

options.text: Liquid, since 20 degrees C is above its melting point
options.rationale: Only the melting point is compared, so the substance is called a liquid.

options.text: Solid, because both quoted values are below zero
options.rationale: The minus signs are read as meaning the substance is cold and therefore solid.

options.text: Liquid, which is normal at room temperature
options.rationale: Liquid is treated as the default state at room temperature instead of being worked out.

options.text: Gas, since 20 degrees C is above its boiling point
options.rationale: Above the boiling point the substance is a gas, whatever sign the quoted values carry.

mcqs.stem: Sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees C but chlorine melts at -101 degrees C. Which explanation of this difference is correct?

options.text: Sodium chloride has strong ionic attractions to break
options.rationale: Different bonding gives forces of very different strengths, so far more energy is needed to melt the ionic lattice.

options.text: The covalent bonds inside chlorine break easily as it melts
options.rationale: Melting a molecular substance is thought to break the covalent bonds inside the molecules.

options.text: Chlorine has fewer bonds, so it melts a lot sooner
options.rationale: Bonds are counted rather than compared for strength.

options.text: Sodium chloride particles are much heavier than chlorine
options.rationale: Particle mass is used in place of the strength of the bonding.

mcqs.stem: A student says that one copper atom is shiny, can be bent and conducts electricity. Why is this wrong?

options.text: A single atom is shiny but it cannot conduct
options.rationale: Some bulk properties are kept for the single atom while others are dropped.

options.text: Bulk properties belong to whole structures
options.rationale: Properties such as shine, malleability and conductivity come from very many atoms arranged and bonded together.

options.text: Only atoms that are inside a compound gain them
options.rationale: Bulk properties are thought to appear when atoms combine chemically.

options.text: An atom is too small to see, so nothing is known
options.rationale: Size of the atom is offered instead of the reason the properties do not apply.

mcqs.stem: What does the state symbol (aq) tell you about a substance in an equation?

options.text: It is a liquid, whether or not it is water
options.rationale: (aq) and (l) are treated as two ways of writing the same thing.

options.text: It is the water used as the solvent here
options.rationale: The symbol is attached to the solvent rather than to the dissolved substance.

options.text: It is a gas bubbled through the mixture
options.rationale: The symbol is guessed from the appearance of a reaction rather than its meaning.

options.text: It is dissolved in water to give a solution
options.rationale: (aq) shows an aqueous solution, that is a substance dissolved in water.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium ribbon is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation has the correct state symbols?

options.text: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
options.rationale: The metal is solid, the acid and the salt are dissolved in water, and hydrogen is given off as a gas.

options.text: Mg(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)
options.rationale: The solid metal is labelled with the state of the mixture it is added to.

options.text: Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(s) + H2(g)
options.rationale: The salt is written as a solid because it is not seen while it stays in solution.

options.text: Mg(s) + 2HCl(l) → MgCl2(s) + H2(g)
options.rationale: The acid is labelled (l) because it can be poured, rather than (aq) because it is a solution.

mcqs.stem: Calcium carbonate chips react with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation has the correct state symbols?

options.text: CaCO3(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(aq) + CO2(g)
options.rationale: The solid carbonate is labelled (aq) because it is put into a solution.

options.text: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
options.rationale: The chips are solid, the acid and the salt are aqueous, the water is a pure liquid and carbon dioxide is a gas.

options.text: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(aq) + CO2(g)
options.rationale: Water is written (aq) because the word aqueous is associated with water itself.

options.text: CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(l) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g)
options.rationale: The dilute acid is labelled (l) because it is a pourable liquid.

mcqs.stem: Why is sodium chloride described as a giant ionic lattice?

options.text: It is built from millions of NaCl molecules joined up
options.rationale: The formula is read as a molecule, and the solid as those molecules stacked together.

options.text: Every sodium ion is attracted to just one chloride ion
options.rationale: The single electron transfer in a bonding diagram keeps the two ions paired for good.

options.text: Very many ions sit in a regular repeating pattern
options.rationale: An ionic compound has a regular structure in which very many oppositely charged ions are held in all directions.

options.text: The electrostatic forces act along the rows of ions
options.rationale: The lines drawn between nearest neighbours are read as directional bonds.

mcqs.stem: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points and boiling points?

options.text: Breaking the many strong bonds needs large amounts of energy
options.rationale: This is the reason given by the specification for the high melting and boiling points of ionic compounds.

options.text: The ions are heavy and packed so tightly they cannot move
options.rationale: Close packing, which is visible in a diagram, is used instead of the strength of the attraction.

options.text: Every ion in the lattice repels the ions beside it
options.rationale: Repulsion between like charges is remembered without noticing that neighbours are oppositely charged.

options.text: The ions must be split into atoms before it can melt
options.rationale: Melting is thought to involve changing the particles rather than separating them.

mcqs.stem: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Why?

options.text: Melting releases electrons that can move through the liquid
options.rationale: The explanation used for metals, where electrons carry the charge, is reused for an ionic compound.

options.text: In the liquid the ions are free to move and carry charge
options.rationale: When melted, the ions are no longer held in fixed positions, so charge can flow.

options.text: Melting turns the neutral particles into charged ions
options.rationale: The ions are thought to be created by melting rather than freed by it.

options.text: Liquids conduct just like water does, but solids never can
options.rationale: Temperature itself is offered as the reason for conduction.

mcqs.stem: Sodium chloride is dissolved in water. Why does the solution conduct electricity?

options.text: Water itself is a very good conductor of electricity
options.rationale: Safety warnings about water and electricity are remembered as chemistry.

options.text: Dissolving splits the molecules into atoms
options.rationale: The solid is treated as molecular, and dissolving as a chemical change.

options.text: The ions separate and are free to move about
options.rationale: Dissolving frees the ions from the lattice so that charge can flow.

options.text: The water supplies free electrons to the mixture
options.rationale: Electrons are assumed to be the charge carriers in every conductor.

mcqs.stem: Why are substances made of small molecules usually gases or liquids at room temperature?

options.text: Their covalent bonds are weak and break very easily
options.rationale: The weak forces between molecules are confused with the strong bonds inside them.

options.text: Their molecules are light enough to float away
options.rationale: Lightness is linked with rising, and rising with being a gas.

options.text: There are no forces at all between the molecules
options.rationale: Nothing is drawn between molecules, so nothing is assumed to be there.

options.text: Only weak forces hold the molecules together
options.rationale: Substances made of small molecules have only weak intermolecular forces, so little energy is needed to separate the molecules.

mcqs.stem: When liquid water boils, what is overcome?

options.text: The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen
options.rationale: The bonds inside the molecule are assumed to be what the energy breaks.

options.text: The intermolecular forces between the water molecules
options.rationale: It is the intermolecular forces, not the covalent bonds, that are overcome when a substance boils.

options.text: Both the covalent bonds and the forces between them
options.rationale: Energy is thought to be shared between breaking bonds and separating molecules.

options.text: The molecules split into hydrogen and oxygen
options.rationale: A change of state is confused with a chemical change.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about a substance made of small molecules is correct?

options.text: Covalent bonds are the weakest forces in the substance
options.rationale: The relative strengths of the two kinds of attraction are reversed.

options.text: Intermolecular forces act inside each molecule
options.rationale: The prefix inter- is confused with intra-.

options.text: Intermolecular forces are weaker than covalent bonds
options.rationale: The intermolecular forces between molecules are weak compared with the covalent bonds inside them.

options.text: There are no forces at all between the molecules
options.rationale: Nothing is drawn between molecules, so nothing is assumed to act between them.

mcqs.stem: Methane, CH4, boils at -162 degrees C while octane, C8H18, boils at 126 degrees C. Why is octane's boiling point so much higher?

options.text: Octane molecules are heavier, so they need more heat energy
options.rationale: Particle mass is used in place of the strength of the intermolecular forces.

options.text: Octane has more covalent bonds that must be broken first
options.rationale: The extra bonds in the larger molecule are assumed to be what the energy breaks.

options.text: Octane is a liquid, and liquids always boil high
options.rationale: The state at room temperature is offered as the cause rather than the consequence.

options.text: Its molecules are larger, so the forces are stronger
options.rationale: Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher boiling points.

mcqs.stem: Why does liquid octane not conduct electricity?

options.text: Its molecules have no overall electric charge
options.rationale: Conduction needs charged particles free to move, and molecules are neutral overall.

options.text: It has no metal atoms to carry the charge along
options.rationale: Conduction is assumed to require a metal.

options.text: Liquids are not able to conduct electricity at all
options.rationale: Conduction is associated only with solid metals.

options.text: Its electrons are locked inside the atoms themselves
options.rationale: The absence of free electrons is offered instead of the absence of charge on the molecules.

mcqs.stem: The bonds inside a Cl2 molecule are strong, yet chlorine boils at -34 degrees C. Which statement explains this?

options.text: The strong covalent bonds break as the chlorine boils
options.rationale: The strong bonds inside the molecule are assumed to be broken on boiling.

options.text: Some covalent bonds break and some are left whole
options.rationale: The energy is thought to be shared between the two kinds of attraction.

options.text: Boiling only has to overcome weak forces between molecules
options.rationale: The strong covalent bonds are not broken; only the weak intermolecular forces are overcome.

options.text: Chlorine molecules have nothing holding them close
options.rationale: The low boiling point is read as meaning there are no intermolecular forces.

mcqs.stem: Why is poly(ethene) a solid at room temperature?

options.text: Covalent bonds join each polymer chain to the next one
options.rationale: The strength of the material is credited to covalent bonds between the chains.

options.text: It is a giant covalent structure just like diamond
options.rationale: Polymers and giant covalent structures are treated as the same category.

options.text: Its molecules are far too heavy to move at all
options.rationale: The mass of the molecule is used in place of the forces between molecules.

options.text: Its very large molecules attract each other strongly
options.rationale: Because polymer molecules are very large, the intermolecular forces between them are relatively strong.

mcqs.stem: A diagram shows a long chain of carbon atoms joined by covalent bonds, with the chain continuing at both ends. What does it show?

options.text: A polymer built from large molecules
options.rationale: Continuation marks and a repeating covalently bonded chain identify a polymer molecule.

options.text: A giant covalent structure such as silica
options.rationale: Any large covalently bonded network is read as a giant covalent structure.

options.text: A metal, since the atoms lie in a line
options.rationale: The layers of a metal are recalled from a similar looking diagram.

options.text: A small molecule such as ethene gas
options.rationale: The repeat unit is read as the whole molecule and the continuation marks are ignored.

mcqs.stem: Why does silicon dioxide have a very high melting point?

options.text: Its intermolecular forces are very strong
options.rationale: The rule learned for small molecules is applied to a giant covalent structure.

options.text: Strong covalent bonds must be overcome
options.rationale: All the atoms in a giant covalent structure are linked by strong covalent bonds, which must be overcome to melt it.

options.text: Strong forces hold its oppositely charged ions
options.rationale: A giant structure with a high melting point is assumed to be ionic.

options.text: Its atoms are heavy and hard to pull apart
options.rationale: Atomic mass is used in place of the strength of the bonding.

mcqs.stem: A diagram shows every carbon atom bonded to four other carbon atoms in a continuous network. What does the diagram show?

options.text: A very large molecule of carbon, like C60
options.rationale: A large covalent network is read as one big molecule instead.

options.text: A giant metallic lattice of carbon atoms
options.rationale: A regular network of identical atoms is matched to the picture of a metal.

options.text: A lattice of oppositely charged ions
options.rationale: A giant lattice is assumed to be made of ions.

options.text: A giant covalent structure, such as diamond
options.rationale: Every atom linked to other atoms by covalent bonds throughout the structure identifies a giant covalent structure.

mcqs.stem: Why do most metals have high melting points and boiling points?

options.text: The metallic bonding in the giant structure is strong
options.rationale: Metals have giant structures of atoms with strong metallic bonding, so most have high melting and boiling points.

options.text: The atoms in a metal are heavy and packed very tightly
options.rationale: Mass and packing are used in place of the strength of the bonding.

options.text: Metals are hard, and hard materials melt slowly
options.rationale: Hardness and melting point are treated as the same property.

options.text: Delocalised electrons stop the atoms escaping
options.rationale: Delocalised electrons are used to explain every property of a metal.

mcqs.stem: Why is an alloy usually harder than the pure metal it is made from?

options.text: The two metals react to make a new compound entirely
options.rationale: Mixing two metals is assumed to be a chemical reaction.

options.text: Atoms of different sizes stop the layers sliding
options.rationale: In a pure metal the atoms are arranged in layers that can slide; different sized atoms disrupt those layers.

options.text: The alloy contains far more delocalised electrons
options.rationale: Delocalised electrons are offered as the explanation for hardness.

options.text: The added atoms are heavier and much harder
options.rationale: The hardness of the alloy is credited to the added atoms being hard in themselves.

mcqs.stem: Why are metals good conductors of electricity and of thermal energy?

options.text: The metal ions are free to move around the metal
options.rationale: The explanation for a molten ionic compound is reused for a solid metal.

options.text: The atoms are packed so tightly that energy passes
options.rationale: Close packing is offered as the whole explanation.

options.text: Delocalised electrons carry charge and energy
options.rationale: The delocalised electrons carry electrical charge through the metal and also transfer thermal energy.

options.text: Protons in the metal carry the electric charge along
options.rationale: Current is associated with positive charge, so the positive particles are assumed to move.
